title: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources' says Kremlin advisor
description: Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin, says there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sha
body: Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin, says there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing military blueprints with Russia.His comments on BBC Newsnight come as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to lobby US President Trump on Ukraine's defence needs. In an interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said, "I'm looking forward to going to New York in September," when the UN General Assembly will meet.He said that while the details were not "fully confirmed", it is "likely" he will go. The trip would be his first to the US since becoming prime minister in July. "Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said following his official visit to Ukraine on Monday, during which he promised to continue pressuring Russia.The UK has also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.Fedorov, who is Russia's former deputy foreign minister, said Putin was facing "serious" pressure "to undertake certain measures against UK". Asked on BBC Newsnight where the pressure was coming from, Fedorov responded, "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media". Asked what a "semi-military" response might look like, Fedorov said "it could take the form of something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine." "They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources," he said.The comments are in line with those made by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday, when he criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them."Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"Burnham's visit to Ukraine was his first official international visit. He met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine in the wake of escalating Russian strikes in recent weeks - including one last week on a shopping centre that killed at least 16 people.Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles, but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.Zelensky has said he is hoping to secure 300 patriot missiles ahead of winter, when Russia is likely to increase its attacks on energy infrastructure, as it has done in past years. In the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said that he felt "really confident" that the issue was "fixable". But he pointed out that it wasn't only the US who could supply Ukraine with Patriots. "There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with," he said. "It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."In July this year, three weeks after offering Ukraine the right to produce Patriots itself, Trump backtracked, saying, "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."  "These weapons are incredible. We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump told a cabinet meeting. In a joint statement after the meeting in Ukraine, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet".In a statement ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes."I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

schema.headline: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources' says Kremlin advisor

title: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Pan Am Flight 103 was brought down on 21 December 1988ByScotland home affairs correspondentThe trial of a Libyan m
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Pan Am Flight 103 was brought down on 21 December 1988ByScotland home affairs correspondentThe trial of a Libyan man over the Lockerbie bombing has been postponed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago.Jury selection was due to get under way in Washington DC on Wednesday but the BBC understands a new start date has been set for January next year.Lawyers acting for Abu Agila Mohammad Kheir Al-Marimi said "newly discovered evidence" previously unknown to the defence and prosecutors from the US government emerged on Friday 21 August.Al-Marimi has denied building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 on December 21, 1988, killing 270 people.His lawyers told the court: "Constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development."They said they met Al-Marimi on Sunday and he agreed that they should ask for the postponement.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has been in custody since December 2022The trial judge, Dabney Friedrich, has agreed that the start date should be set aside, underlining the potential importance of the new evidence.She would have been extremely reluctant to allow an 11th hour postponement after months of preparation and marathon pre-trial legal battles.For the relatives of those who died and Al-Marimi himself, this latest delay means a verdict might not come until next spring.It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns over nearly four decades.Pan Am 103 was flying from Heathrow to New York when the bomb exploded in its forward hold, breaking the plane apart at 31,000 feet.All 259 passengers and crew on board were killed.  Another 11 people died in Lockerbie when the wreckage fell on their homes.Of the victims, 190 were American and 43 from the UK.Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the worst terror attack and mass murder in British history.'Disappointing for the families'Al-Marimi has been in US custody since 2022 and was originally due to stand trial in May 2025.That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Al-Marimi's ill health.The trial was pencilled in for April this year but was called off again, after the defence asked for more time to prepare.The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988.Prosecutors from the Crown Office and detectives from Police Scotland were due to travel to Washington to attend the case, and Scottish witnesses were expected to be among the first to give evidence at the trial.Laura Buchan, head of the Lockerbie investigation team at the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service said:  "I recognise that this adjournment will be disappointing for the families and for those who have followed this case over many years."As the matter remains before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the reasons for the adjournment. Although these proceedings are being led by the United States authorities, Scottish prosecutors and police officers remain fully committed to supporting the pursuit of justice."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was the only man convicted of the Lockerbie bombingA grandfather in his 70s, Al-Marimi has been accused of carrying out the attack along with two Libyans who faced a Scottish court in May 2000.Three judges heard the case at Camp Zeist, a former US air force base in the Netherlands.After eight months, they ruled the atrocity was an act of state sponsored terrorism carried out by members of the Libyan intelligence service.The judges convicted one of the Libyans, Abdulbasset Al-Megrahi, of mass murder and jailed him for life.He died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government.The Scottish Criminal Cases Review Conviction twice referred Megrahi's case to the appeal court but the conviction was upheld.The second Libyan, Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was acquitted and returned home to a hero's welcome in Tripoli.The US government says Al-Marimi admitted bombing the plane along with Megrahi and Fhimah when he was questioned in a Libyan detention facility in 2012.The alleged confession was handed to Scottish investigators in 2017 and is now central to the prosecution case.Al-Marimi has claimed the confession is false and was made under duress, but judge Friedrich ruled it can be admitted as evidence at the trial.

schema.headline: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start

title: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?
description: Speaking in June last year to British businesswoman and podcaster Emma Grede, Meghan talked about her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, and
body: Speaking in June last year to British businesswoman and podcaster Emma Grede, Meghan talked about her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, and hinted at a return to acting when asked if she missed that side to her life."Sometimes," Meghan replied. "Being back on set with With Love, Meghan was great because I realised how much I miss my crew. I love being around a crew."But Variety's chief correspondent Marlow Stern says when it comes to deliberations over a potential acting role for Meghan, "a lot of it has to do with scheduling, to be honest"."They're maybe also negotiating the size of the role and how many days she'll shoot, and also compensation for it. Both sides often play the media to try and push things along, and we could be seeing that."For Harry, the focus once back in the UK will be on the charity work and patronages he has kept hold of while living thousands of miles away.He has now completed his final charity engagements in the US before flying back to the UK in the coming days.In Washington DC, he met military veterans and their families and visited America's main hospital for injured servicemen and women, Walter Reed National Military Medical Centre.At Arlington National Cemetery, he visited the final resting place of many service personal killed in Iraq and Afghanistan wars where he himself served on two operational tours.At the grave of Sergeant Michael Verardo, who died last year from complications related to injuries sustained in Afghanistan in 2010, he met Verardo's widow Sarah - who now supports other military families - and their nine-year-old daughter, Elizabeth.The couple will keep their multi-million dollar home in Montecito, about a two-hour drive north of Los Angeles. Meghan's mother, Doria Ragland, who has been heavily involved in helping to care for her grandchildren, will remain living in California.The family is expected to return to the US regularly as well as use the holiday home they have bought near Melides in Portugal. It is close to a property bought by Princess Eugenie and her husband Jack Brooksbank who have remained close to the Sussexes during the royal fallout.How involved Harry, Meghan, Archie and Lilibet will be with the wider royal family has not yet been decided.Over the next few months, several significant royal engagements are in the diary that would involve most senior royals - Remembrance Sunday at the Cenotaph, the Princess of Wales' Carol Service at Westminster Abbey and then Christmas at Sandringham.Will there be invitations extended to the Sussex family?Trust remains an issue. There is caution, a degree of wariness and even hostility in some quarters of the Royal Household. These decisions are very much a work in progress.Harry and Meghan's team has described the move to the UK as being for "an extended period of time".It is not necessarily a long-term move but may be a chance for the family to experience life in the UK, allowing the children to get to know their grandfather, the King, while they are young enough to not have their education disrupted.Much of what happens in the months ahead will be a test - of Harry and Meghan's liking for life in the UK, of public reaction to them and of the royal family's ability to continue with their duties alongside the distractions the Sussex family may bring.Additional reporting by James Govan.

schema.headline: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?

title: Thousands of social and affordable homes to be built across England in £39bn plan
description: Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allo
body: Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost £10bn, in a bid to address the housing crisis.Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool, as well as £6bn for London.It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes across the nation, under the government's £39bn social housebuilding programme.Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".Of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "No child should be raised in a hostel room and no family should wait 10 years for a front door of their own. I have said from my first day in this job that everything starts with a good home."Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Burnham had called for the entire 10-year £39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent.Under Labour, homeless figures have continued to rise to record levels.Data released earlier this month suggested 177,530 children were homeless in temporary accommodation.Natasha, who has been living in a hotel in Milton Keynes for the last four months with her son Zayd, is one of those waiting for a permanent home.The 22-year-old spent the final months of her pregnancy and the first weeks of her son's life living in a hotel.She says she has no idea how long she will be expected to stay there but was told it would only be temporary. "I'm just scared when he gets older, when he starts crawling around, I can't even allow him to crawl in such a place like that because it's so dirty," she says. While pregnant, Natasha says her room became infested with ants, which she repeatedly reported before eventually being moved into another room.But her problems didn't end there. While Natasha has her own bathroom, she shares a kitchen with around 60 other residents. She says the hotel is home to a mix of people, not just mothers and babies, and that she does not always feel safe using the shared space with Zayd.Natasha describes living there as feeling "like a prison". She says visitors are not allowed, meaning friends and family can not come to help her with her five-week-old boy."I just want somewhere peaceful for him and calm. Somewhere nice where I can bring him up," she says. She is one of the 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists as of March 2025, the latest government figures.London will see the largest share of funding, although no figure has been given for how many homes will be built in the capital.Ministers said Monday's allocation was the first stage of the 10-year programme and more than £16bn remains to be allocated outside London.Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested some of the new homes will be built by councils, saying she and the prime minister were "doing everything we can to get councils building once again".Burnham had previously promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period", and the government said millions extra would be given to councils to support their housebuilding plans and help with expertise.But the announcement stops short of clarifying how the funding will be split between council homes and those provided by housing associations.In the 1950s, councils were building almost 200,000 new council homes a year, but half of councils do not currently own or build their own homes.In 2024-25, there were just over 12,000 homes built for social rent - the highest since 2013 -14, but organisations like the National Housing Federation and homeless charities have previously agreed that at least 90,000 social homes would need to be built each year to meet demand.Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.Charlie Berry, policy manager at housing charity Shelter, said the announcement was "not near the level we need to truly tackle that backlog and end homelessness".But she said it was a "significant improvement", and added she would "love" Rayner to commit to a target of how many socially rented homes will be built annually.As well as promise and funding to build more social homes, the Labour government pledged to build 1.5 million homes by 2029.Despite statements like "build, baby, build", coined by former housing secretary Steve Reed, so far Labour is not on track to meet that target.BBC Verify has been tracking the target using government statistics on the number of Energy Performance Certificates (EPC) issued by each local authority. Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.The latest EPC data suggests about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England in the 12 months ending June 2026. To reach the government's target of 1.5 million homes over five years, there would need to be at least 300,000.Conservative shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly described the announcement as "sleight of hand", saying: "The small print shows homes won't have to be delivered until 2039."He said: "Fewer homes will be delivered than previous programmes in this Parliament as social rent is more expensive. Labour have scaled back their affordable housing programme and expect us to thank them for it."The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election which they estimated would "free up" 228,144 homes for "British families". On Monday, Reform announced similar plans to prioritise British-born workers under 35 when allocating social housing if it were to enter government.Shelter said there were "already strict rules on who can access social housing" and neither plan addressed the underlying cause of the problems.

schema.headline: Thousands of social and affordable homes to be built across England in £39bn plan

title: US-Canada trade war heats up as Trump threatens to hike auto tariffs
description: US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump threatens tariff hike on autos after Carney vows to retaliate Figure caption, Watch: "Absolutely ridiculous": C
body: US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump threatens tariff hike on autos after Carney vows to retaliate Figure caption, Watch: "Absolutely ridiculous": Canadians react to new tariff tensions with the USByNadine YousifSenior Canada reporterUpdated 1 hour agoPresident Donald Trump has threatened to hike US tariffs on automobiles originating in Canada, as the trade war between the two neighbours continues to heat up.Trump said on Monday that he will increase tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as auto parts, from 25% to 50% as of 1 January. It comes after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making unreasonable last-minute demands.Late on Monday, Canada officials announced a news conference on Tuesday where they would outline how the country would respond to the trade war and work to "protect and support Canadian workers and businesses during these challenging times". The news conference at 09:00 ET (14:00 BST) will include government leaders in business, finance and economic development. Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney called Trump's latest levy threat unsurprising and accused the president of wanting to destroy Canada's auto industry.  He added that Canada is ready to resume talks only if the US comes with the "right attitude".The war of words followed several US and Canadian officials saying that talks were suspended with no set date to resume.Canada walked away from trade negotiations late on Friday night, moments before a US-imposed deadline that would add a 50% levy on nearly $20bn (C$28bn; £14bn) of Canadian imports.The collapse in talks marked a significant change in tone from earlier in the week, when both sides appeared optimistic that a new US-Canada trade deal could be reached.Figure caption, Watch: Canada will negotiate if US has the "right attitude", says Mark CarneyCanadian officials have said the US introduced last-minute demands that were "unacceptable", including a clause limiting which countries Canada could sign trade deals with.US officials, meanwhile, said it was Canada that introduced last-minute changes. "They wanted more," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview with CNBC on Monday. The breakdown led to growing tensions as both sides publicly dug in their heels. On Monday, Trump's tariff threats to Canada's auto industry followed Carney declaring the country would counter his levies with reciprocal tariffs on US goods "dollar for dollar". 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade warHow Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and TrumpTrump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapseCarney said he was focused on supporting Canadian businesses impacted by new 50% US tariffs after the Friday deadline expired, as well as building infrastructure to diversify Canada's trade, which historically has relied heavily on the US. Carney announced funding of C$11bn ($7.95bn; £5.83bn) to build six icebreakers at a Quebec shipyard for the Canadian Coast Guard that will replace its medium and heavy ageing fleet. The icebreakers will be used to open winter shipping routes through Canada's northern and Atlantic waters.Figure caption, 'Trump underestimates us': Doug Ford takes aim at US over tariffsMeanwhile, Ontario's outspoken premier, Doug Ford, whose province is home to Canada's auto manufacturing industry, responded to Trump's tariffs and threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass". Ford also suggested that Canada should charge the US extra for its oil and gas, as well as electricity and critical minerals, adding that he will be speaking to Carney on ways to "fight back".His comments appeared to catch the attention of Trump, who in a Truth Social post accused Ford of "bluster" and wrote: "Someone should get these clowns to 'fall in line' or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!".Canada accounts for 60% of total US crude oil imports and close to 100% of US natural gas exports, according to Canadian government data.Figure caption, Watch: Brewery owner tells BBC tariff impact will be "devastating"Businesses on both sides have warned that they stand to be hurt by the new wave of US tariffs on Canada, as well as the retaliatory tariffs that Canada plans to impose on 8 September. In Portland, Oregon, Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing say the price of one of their best-selling items - specially designed pillows made in Canada - could shoot up by around 50% to $90. For now, they are holding out on keeping the prices steady, hoping that the "tariff problem" is worked out soon, said Roach. "It would be one thing if we had three months' notice - that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors," he said. "But when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck." The rapidly escalating trade war is also raising questions about the other country in North America - Mexico - and the trade pact between the three neighbours known as the USMCA.Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form. The pact underpins $1.6tn in North American Trade.Escalating trade tensions mean "the risk of the USMCA unravelling has increased",  experts from the Oxford Economics forecasting firm warned on Monday. That, in turn, "would plunge Canada into recession and leave it on a permanently lower growth path".Additional reporting by Ana Faguy.

schema.headline: US-Canada trade war heats up as Trump threatens to hike auto tariffs

title: Asbestos cancer killed mum in her 40s – was her school to blame?
description: Figure caption, 'Mum died young from asbestos - now my family want justice'ByWill FyfeWales Impact and Angharad ThomasBBC WalesWhen Caroline Bryan was
body: Figure caption, 'Mum died young from asbestos - now my family want justice'ByWill FyfeWales Impact and Angharad ThomasBBC WalesWhen Caroline Bryan was enjoying high school with friends in the early 90s, she would never have imagined replaying those memories in her final weeks, while searching for answers about her terminal condition.The mum was 46 when she died from mesothelioma, an incurable cancer linked to asbestos exposure.As she came to terms with her difficult diagnosis, Caroline's belief was the only place she could have encountered asbestos was during her time at school decades earlier.Her family blame the local authority that ran Caroline's school for her death and are taking legal action. Cardiff council said it would be inappropriate to comment on ongoing legal proceedings."She never had the sort of career that would have exposed her to asbestos," said Caroline's daughter Brooklyn."We never lived in any houses that would have had asbestos in."Caroline was mostly a stay at home mum and the family hadn't heard of mesothelioma before, but quickly learned it likely came from asbestos fibres she will have unknowingly breathed in many years before.Image source, Brooklyn BryanImage caption, Brooklyn said she remembered her mum as a "kind and caring person" who would go "above and beyond for anybody""Before she passed, she contacted a solicitor," added Brooklyn."She wanted justice - not just for herself, but to stop anyone else going through the same thing."The 26-year-old said her world "turned upside down" when she found out her mum had incurable cancer. Brooklyn said after looking back through her mum's life, they began to believe she was exposed to asbestos at her old high school, the old Fitzalan site in Cardiff.The family's legal team helped to uncover council documents which they say show asbestos was used "quite extensively" at the site during Caroline's time there in the 1990s."Mum mentioned that the building wasn't in good condition," said Brooklyn.Image source, Brooklyn BryanImage caption, Caroline was 45 years old when she noticed she was having breathing difficulties "Things like ceiling tiles were broken. There was dust and debris when things were disturbed, though at the time she didn't know what it was."Caroline had only gone to the doctors because she'd noticed a shortness of breath. In her mid 40s, she was far younger than most mesothelioma patients. Doctors had initially told Caroline she could have a few years left – but she passed away just three months after her diagnosis, aged 46."I was 23," said Brooklyn."Suddenly, I had to take over everything—running the house, paying bills, cooking, cleaning. She had always looked after me, so I wasn't used to doing those things. I was essentially forced into adulthood overnight. It was very difficult."Losing your mum, who is your main support system, at that age is incredibly hard. Now she's gone, I feel I have to continue this [fight] for her."Caroline's family are bringing a High Court claim against Cardiff council over her death, with the case set to be heard in early 2027.Image caption, Brooklyn Bryan believes her mum was exposed to asbestos as a teenager at secondary school"The council's own documents show that asbestos was used quite extensively in that school," said Phillip Gower from Redkite Solicitors, who are representing the family."The buildings were in pretty poor condition, with damage to the walls around the doors, the floor tiles, the ceiling tiles."Cardiff Council said it would "not be appropriate" to comment on Caroline's case but it recognised the "devastating impact" of mesothelioma on patients and families. "We would like to reassure parents, staff and the wider public that the management of asbestos in Cardiff council buildings, including schools, is taken extremely seriously," added a spokesperson. Many primary and secondary schools were built using asbestos, a common building material until its dangers became clear and it was banned in the UK in 1999.Most schools still contain some asbestos and authorities must regularly inspect it to check it has not been damaged and at risk of releasing tiny fibres into the air, which can cause cancers like mesothelioma.A Freedom of Information request by BBC Wales suggested more than three quarters of schools in Wales still contained asbestos.Responses from 20 of Wales' 22 local authorities showed 76% of primary schools and 81% of secondary schools had asbestos containing materials (ACMs).Image caption, Fitzalan High School pupils were taught at the same site Caroline attended from 1964 until the 1,800-pupil school moved to new premises in 2023Mesothelioma is the 20th most common type of cancer in the UK, responsible for 2,200 deaths per year, according to Cancer Research UK.It can develop from a single asbestos fibre lodged in the lungs, often unknowingly breathed in many decades earlier.It is more common in men, particularly those who have worked in heavy industry or trades where they would have regular contact with asbestos. Most deaths from the disease happen when people are in their 80s.However, an epidemiologist who has spent decades studying mesothelioma rates, said there were two "concerning epidemiological observations" coming from more recent data."First, the number of mesothelioma cases per year [in people] under the age of 40 in Britain has increased over the last 5 or 6 years - it' increased from 2.5 cases per year to 5 cases per year," said Professor Julian Peto. "The second thing is that there is a slightly but significantly increased mesothelioma risk in female teachers."Peto said the findings were "not conclusive" but did "raise concern".Image source, Brooklyn BryanImage caption, Brooklyn Bryan said her mum Caroline could make "any situation better" when she was growing upHe said there were two likely causes. Either the removal of large amounts of asbestos in schools in the 1980s had accidentally exposed more people to its dangerous fibres – or asbestos in the buildings was deteriorating and releasing more fibres over time, exposing to later generations of pupils and teachers.Peto said more data was needed to see what was happening – but depending on the answer it could mean more asbestos needs to be removed from schools or that removing it could be the very thing causing the exposure.Often, when someone is diagnosed with mesothelioma they are given a list of solicitors to contact by medical staff so they can look into whether they are due compensation."We are now seeing more women, most of whom cannot readily identify where they could have been exposed to asbestos," said Richard Green from Hugh James Solicitors."What we are also starting to see is a number of younger people who are suffering with mesothelioma. In the last 12 months or so, we've definitely seen an increase in the number of people coming forward who are under 50."Green, a partner in the firm's asbestos litigation team, said they'd seen three mesothelioma clients under 40 years old in the past few months – but that it was still exceptionally rare to see anyone under 50 with the disease.He said until around a decade ago most cases were men who'd spent their carers working with asbestos – but his firm now considers claims from people who believe they were exposed in schools, either as teachers or pupils.Helen Wilson said it was "devastating" to hear her sister Linda Langhelt had been diagnosed with mesothelioma.Image source, Helen WilsonImage caption, Linda Langhelt's family believe she could have been exposed to asbestos while working as a teacher, decades before her death from cancerThe retired science teacher, who spent her career working in Cardiff and Essex, had gone to see her GP about a shortness of breath thinking it could be "heart problems" before being given her diagnosis."The hospital said she could have contracted it 20 or 30 years before," said her younger sister Helen."The horrible thing about mesothelioma is that you haven't a clue that you've got it until it's too late."Helen said that as a biology teacher, Linda knew exactly what her diagnosis meant – but stayed "stoic" until the end.She died aged 82, 18 months after finding out about her mesothelioma."Every one of us has been in buildings from time to time that have asbestos in them," said Helen.The Welsh Government said the safety of pupils and staff was of "paramount importance"."We continue to support local authorities through investment in school buildings, practical guidance and close collaboration with the Health and Safety Executive and Ystadau Cymru to ensure schools remain safe, modern and fit for purpose," said a spokesperson. Cardiff Council added that it had "robust and well-established" plans to manage asbestos in its buildings. "Council buildings are surveyed, asbestos records are maintained and regularly reviewed, and checks are carried out to monitor the condition of any known asbestos-containing materials," said a spokesperson."We remain committed to providing safe environments for pupils, staff and visitors and will continue to manage asbestos in accordance with all current legal requirements and recognised best practice."Get in touchHave you been affected by issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: Asbestos cancer killed mum in her 40s – was her school to blame?

title: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workersByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing, Hangzhou and Chengdu"I
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workersByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing, Hangzhou and Chengdu"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.Image caption, Students learning robotics at the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of many new vocational schoolsIt is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.Image caption, More than two millions robots work alongside people in China's factories On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code."Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."Image caption, Pang Kai is part of the research and development teamA shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages."In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotor.Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."Image caption, Machines are part of every step in making Leapmotor's EVsChina has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand."China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics."If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.Image caption, Chinese innovation is powering the country's factories faster than expected   And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says."It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption. It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

schema.headline: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding

title: US Open 2026 qualifying results: Heather Watson among British winners in New York
description: Britain's Heather Watson battled back from a set down against Claire Liu to keep alive her hopes of securing a first US Open main-draw appearance in f
body: Britain's Heather Watson battled back from a set down against Claire Liu to keep alive her hopes of securing a first US Open main-draw appearance in five years.The 34-year-old Watson beat sixth seed Liu 4-6 6-2 6-4 in the first round of qualifying in New York.Watson almost let a double-break lead slip in the final set but held firm to set up a meeting with Spain's Angela Fita Boluda.Toby Samuel, Jacob Fearnley, Billy Harris and Harry Wendelken all progressed in men's qualifying.Samuel, seeking to reach the US Open main draw for the first time, fought back against Italy's Francesco Maestrelli to win 6-7 (2-7) 6-3 6-1 and set up a meeting with fellow Briton Harris.Harris progressed with a 6-1 6-3 win against Peru's Gonzalo Bueno.Fearnley claimed a 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 victory over Spain's Roberto Carballes Baena to set up a meeting with Frenchman Luka Pavlovic.Wendelken will meet Swiss player Remy Bertola after overcoming Italy's Stefano Travaglia 6-4 3-6 6-3.However, Liam Broady lost 7-6 (7-4) 6-3 against Italy's Marco Cecchinato, while Felix Gill was beaten by Italian Francesco Passaro 7-6 (7-3) 6-2.Players must come through three rounds of qualifying to reach the singles main draw, which gets under way on Sunday.In the mixed doubles competition, Britons Henry Patten and Lloyd Glasspool will both seek to beat some of the sport's biggest stars after coming through two qualifying matches on Monday.The US Open mixed doubles was controversially revamped last year to include singles stars in a bid to attract more attention to the format.Under the new format, the top six pairs with the best combined singles rankings received direct entry into the main draw, with another eight receiving wildcards.The tournament now takes place over three days in the week before the main draw began, and features a shorter scoring system with only four games required to win a set in matches before the final, no 'advantage' scoring and 10-point match tie-breaks instead of a third set throughout.Both Patten and Glasspool had to come through qualifying with their respective partners on Monday.Patten, a two-time winner of the men's doubles competition at Wimbledon, and Czech team-mate Katerina Siniakova defeated Americans Peyton Stearns and Christian Harrison in straight sets in their second qualifying match.Next, Patten and Siniakova - the respective men's and women's world number ones in doubles - will take on 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic and top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka in the first round of the main draw.After defeating El Salvador's Marcelo Arevalo and France's Kristina Mladenovic, Glasspool and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe will face 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams and seven-time major winner Carlos Alcaraz.Alcaraz will be playing his first match in four months after recovering from a wrist injury, while Williams is making her return to the sport after a four-year absence.

title: Keely Hodgkinson withdraws from Zurich Diamond League as body "not quite ready"
description: Keely Hodgkinson has withdrawn from the women's 800 metres at Thursday's Diamond League meeting in Zurich because her "body is not quite ready".Olympi
body: Keely Hodgkinson has withdrawn from the women's 800 metres at Thursday's Diamond League meeting in Zurich because her "body is not quite ready".Olympic champion Hodgkinson had been set to go head-to-head with Switzerland's Audrey Werro, who beat the Briton to gold at the European Championships in Birmingham earlier this month."Unfortunately the body isn't quite ready to race again after the European Championships," Hodgkinson said in a statement."We've made the decision to skip this race and get ready for the next one. Sad to miss it, hopefully see you next year!"The race will feature world 400m hurdles champion Femke Broeders-Bol, who has stepped up to the 800m this season, and Hodgkinson's training partner Georgia Hunter-Bell, who won 800m gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow last month.World 800m champion Lilian Odira of Kenya, who beat Hodgkinson and Hunter-Bell to gold in Tokyo last year, has pulled out of the race after suffering from illness and weakness since the Commonwealth Games.While Diamond League organisers said they were looking forward to Hodgkinson's "highly anticipated race against Audrey Werro", they "fully respect" the Briton's decision and "hope to see her back in Zurich in the future".After suffering hamstring and knee injuries over the past few years, Hodgkinson skipped the Commonwealth Games to prioritise the European Championships amid a busy summer schedule."I signed myself up for Zurich because I knew everyone was in it but me. I want to be in with the best and I think that's going to bring out the best in me," Hodgkinson said in Birmingham earlier this month.Before winning 800m gold at the London Diamond League on 18 July, Hodgkinson said she was feeling "definitely a lot better than I was".Thursday's meet in Zurich is the penultimate Diamond League event of the season, with the final to take place in Brussels over two days on Friday 4 and Saturday 5 September.

schema.headline: Keely Hodgkinson withdraws from Zurich Diamond League as body "not quite ready"

title: Briton Bradley Townsend killed fighting for Russia in Ukraine
description: Image source, OTHERImage caption, Bradley Townsend left South Yorkshire in April, reportedly telling his family he was going to RomaniaByTom AireyAndr
body: Image source, OTHERImage caption, Bradley Townsend left South Yorkshire in April, reportedly telling his family he was going to RomaniaByTom AireyAndrew Jackson and Corinne WheatleyYorkshireA British national has been killed in Ukraine while fighting for Russia.Bradley Townsend is said to have died following an attack by a remote-controlled FPV drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. His death, on 10 June, is believed to be the first of a British citizen fighting for Russia in the conflict.The 33-year-old left his home in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, earlier this year after telling his family he was going to Romania, according to the Yorkshire Post, external.The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was aware of reports a British national had died in Ukraine, adding it was in contact with his family.The news emerged as Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first foreign trip as UK prime minister.The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of the country's independence from the Soviet Union.The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Andy Burnham has promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats", on his first official visit to Ukraine as UK prime ministerIn a video shared online on 4 April, Townsend featured alongside Ben Stimson and Aiden Minnis - who were given Russian citizenship for fighting in the occupied Donbas region.In the video, uploaded to a Russian recruitment account, Townsend described himself as "a normal working-class lad from Yorkshire".Filmed by Stimson with Minnis interviewing, Townsend discussed the implications of his decision to leave the UK and fight for Russia during the video.He said: "I came with the idea that I probably won't be able to go home, definitely get persecuted if I went back."He later added: "I'm not here for a suicide mission, but I understand that's what can happen."Stimson, from Oldham, and Minnis, from Wiltshire, are believed to be the first British nationals fighting for Russian president Vladimir Putin since he ordered the full scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Stimson was previously jailed in the UK in 2015 for joining pro-Russian separatists in the east of Ukraine.Image source, GMPImage caption, Ben Stimson was jailed in the UK before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine after travelling to join a pro-Russian group in the regionMinnis announced the death of Townsend, using the Yorkshireman's call sign of Badger, in a social media post.The FCDO said it advised against all travel to Russia and "our ability to provide consular support in these circumstances is severely limited".Its foreign travel advice for Ukraine warns travelling to Ukraine to fight or to assist others engaged in the war may amount to offences under UK legislation."You could be prosecuted on your return to the UK," it adds.A number of British nationals have been killed during the war.However, they have all been fighting for Ukraine, following Russia's attacks on the country since 2022.Townsend is thought to be the second man from Yorkshire to die during the war, with 18-year-old James Wilton, from Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, killed in 2024 after he volunteered to fight for Ukraine. title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByMark PoyntingClimate reporterThe world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from huma
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByMark PoyntingClimate reporterThe world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El Niño weather phenomenon.The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life."This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus."El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.The data is based on sea temperatures 10m (32ft 10in) below the surface, using measurements from buoys, ships and satellites, which are combined to produce a global estimate.While the margin of record is currently very small and any global estimate comes with uncertainties, scientists say its timing is particularly notable. Average worldwide sea temperatures tend to reach their yearly peak in March or April, which corresponds to the end of summer in the southern hemisphere - and not in August.The southern hemisphere contains more of the planet's ocean surface than the northern hemisphere and so exerts a bigger influence on average sea temperatures.What is especially concerning to scientists is that the oceans are already so hot when the natural El Niño weather phenomenon is still some way off its expected peak.El Niño brings unusually warm waters to the surface of the eastern and central tropical Pacific Ocean. Warmer waters across such a large area means that global average temperatures typically spike too.El Niño is expected to keep strengthening until Christmas time, with scientists warning that it is on course to be the strongest in centuries.This could see ocean temperatures climb yet further."The fact that we are already breaking records is an early indicator of how strong the El Niño is becoming," said Dr Jeremy Grist, senior research fellow at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton. "All things being equal we might expect the ocean temperature record to be broken again in March [or] April 2027," he added. The waters far away from El Niño's Pacific hunting ground are also extremely warm, including around the UK and Europe.The western English Channel has seen almost continuous marine heatwave conditions for more than three years, peaking at 7C above normal in July, according to Prof Tim Smyth, director of science at Plymouth Marine Laboratory.“This is unprecedented,” he added.Scientists say such widespread warmth around the planet is a clear sign of the growing effect that human-caused climate change is having on the world's seas. The oceans take up more than 90% of the excess heat trapped by humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels. "The latest Copernicus data reinforce the troubling upward trend in ocean temperatures,” said Smyth.Warmer seas help to fuel more extreme weather. They can provide storms with extra moisture and energy, and can intensify heatwaves on land in some coastal regions by reducing the cooling effect of sea breezes.Warmer water also takes up more space, raising sea levels and bringing a greater risk of coastal flooding - while intense ocean heat can be devastating for sea habitats, such as coral reefs.The increasing frequency of marine heatwaves is already "putting increasing pressure on marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on them", Burgess said.Figure caption, Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?Get in touchWhat questions or concerns do you have about El Niño?

title: Aston Villa: Ollie Watkins transfer saga leaves Villa shellshocked
description: Al-Hilal, who have offered close to £40m, are not near to Aston Villa's asking price. As next Tuesday's transfer deadline nears, Villa will play hardb
body: Al-Hilal, who have offered close to £40m, are not near to Aston Villa's asking price. As next Tuesday's transfer deadline nears, Villa will play hardball for their all-time record Premier League goalscorer. A deal is still believed to be some way off, even if Emery revealed last week the striker could leave.Al-Hilal, who signed Crysensio Summerville from West Ham in July, are likely to need to move one of their overseas players to make room for Watkins, despite loaning Darwin Nunez to Diriyah last week, so there are other moving parts in the deal. Watkins has been training on his own, having returned from an extended break following the World Cup and is understood to have made his feelings clear to the Villa hierarchy about moving. There have been no public comments from Watkins or his representatives but he is understood to be open to the move.They have also kept quiet about Emery's response - particularly his enigmatic "silence" answer to Sky Sports' question on why his striker was not involved at Brighton, which appeared to lay the blame at Watkins' door.Another unanswered question is whether Villa see the Saudi money for a striker turning 31 in December - and who had been in and out of Emery's team last season - as a good deal.Perhaps the very real pain at this potential break-up is the reason for the difficulties.The 30-year-old has 108 goals in 278 games for Villa after joining from Brentford for a then-record £28m and has been synonymous with Villa's rise of the past six years. The triumphant night in Istanbul, when Watkins helped Villa end their 30-year wait for a trophy as they beat Freiburg to win the Europa League, currently stand as a crowning glory.His departure would be the most emotional of this summer's big exits - as while Ezri Konsa's influence was crucial, Watkins' goals, work-rate and nature made him one of Villa's poster boys.He is a grounded and family-orientated individual who enjoys the occasional game of golf but always focuses on his football.But he has been in this position before, although at a lower level. Having initially been left out by Paul Tisdale at Exeter amid interest from Derby in 2017, he pleaded with the manager to play and came off the bench to score in a win against Wycombe.Given he has that attitude and desire, those at Villa are surprised at how the relationship with Watkins is ending. It was not expected to be like this.Had it been someone different, a player who had previously not been a manager's dream to work with, Emery's response might have been more indifferent.Along with Watkins, Villa must resolve Martinez's future after a second summer of discontent from the Argentina international.A move to Juventus fell through earlier this month, as they were unwilling to meet Villa's financial demands, and a solution must be found for the 33-year-old after the signing of Zion Suzuki to become the club's number one. Signing a striker to replace Watkins will be harder than sourcing Konsa's replacement - on which Villa are already working, having had two bids rejected by Southampton for Taylor Harwood-Bellis. Brian Madjo's availability, after VIlla won their battle against Fifa to register him, gives Emery an additional option, although at 17 the striker cannot be expected to carry the burden. Villa have been open to letting Tammy Abraham leave but Watkins' increasingly likely departure will have an impact on that thinking. Striker Abraham, who joined from Besiktas in January, has not been looking for any Villa Park exit and remains happy at the club. Nicolas Jackson remains a top target for Emery, who worked with the Chelsea forward at Villarreal, while there has been no direct contact with Manchester United over Joshua Zirkzee.Emery needs to find new heroes after the exits of Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans - two Istanbul goalscorers - along with Lucas Digne and Konsa. But if Watkins goes, his departure will cut the deepest.

schema.headline: Aston Villa: Ollie Watkins transfer saga leaves Villa shellshocked

title: France tornado: dozens injured and hundreds of homes damaged
description: The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials.Authorities in the Aude department in so
body: The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials.Authorities in the Aude department in south-west France cancelled the third stage of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race in the area after a hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced riders to seek shelter.Eyewitness footage from the region captured the swirling vortex of the tornado looming in the horizon above houses and trees.Images from the small village of Pomas, which was the hardest hit, showed uprooted trees, damaged cars and rubble from destroyed homes.Meanwhile there were flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.On average, France experiences several dozen tornadoes per year, according to the country's national weather service Météo-France. It comes after Europe's summer of unprecedented heatwaves and wildfires, with France's south-west region among the worst affected with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.

title: Julian Alvarez transfer news: Arsenal, Barcelona or Atletico Madrid stay for striker?
description: Acrimony, anger and animosity: the Julian Alvarez summer transfer saga in a nutshell.The boos aimed at the Atletico Madrid forward from his own suppor
body: Acrimony, anger and animosity: the Julian Alvarez summer transfer saga in a nutshell.The boos aimed at the Atletico Madrid forward from his own supporters at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium on Sunday provided the latest twist in what has been one of the most bitter - and certainly public - storylines of the window.And with deadline day on 1 September, the Argentine World Cup winner's future remains one of the hottest topics.In simplistic terms the dispute comes down to this: Alvarez wants to join Barcelona - but Atletico won't let him.The Madrid club's steadfast refusal to sanction the 26-year-old's dream move to the Spotify Camp Nou has led to one of the most rancorous public falling-outs in recent memory.The feud led to Atleti fans jeering their own player on his return to club action after the summer World Cup in a 2-2 home draw with Villarreal on Sunday.It had been anticipated.Atletico Madrid president Enrique Cerezo, speaking last week, said: "I don't know if he will say sorry, but Julian is an excellent person and I am absolutely sure that he will win over the fans in two games."I said he wouldn't be sold, he's our player and an important part of our team. We like that he's with us and think he will have a magnificent season."Nevertheless, the events that unfolded on Sunday certainly haven't gone unnoticed at Arsenal.BBC Sport has consistently reported over the summer that Alvarez is viewed as the Gunners' dream transfer target.But for the vast majority of the window, Arsenal's interest has been largely dormant because they were fully aware of his desire to join Barcelona.They have been waiting for the right moment to strike and those at the Emirates are hopeful that time may be coming.But is the deal possible?Arsenal are realistic about their chances of signing Alvarez before next week's transfer deadline.Do they want him? Yes. Are they trying? Yes. Can they pull it off? The answer to that question is less unequivocal.Manager Mikel Arteta and sporting director Andrea Berta know it is a long shot, not least because former Manchester City forward Alvarez, at least so far, has shown little indication he would be willing to join the club.His current reluctance to give the green light on a move to London isn't necessarily linked to any apprehension towards Arsenal - but rather that doing so would see him forgoing his dream of joining Barcelona.Alvarez has also been made aware of certain visa regulations that would create difficulty for his family visiting him in the UK.Moving to Catalonia is what he truly wants. What's more, the Camp Nou club are absolutely willing to make that happen.But Atleti are absolutely adamant they will not sell Alvarez to Barcelona.In May, they made a series of social media posts brutally mocking the pursuit by the Spanish champions of their player to millions of followers."Don't believe everything you see, especially if it's related to Barca," Atletico posted. "In recent months, we've been suffering a smear campaign against one of our players."For the Madrid side, the matter is closed and that leaves Alvarez's dream in serious jeopardy.Therein lies a sliver of hope for Arsenal because, as things stand, the only way out is a move to the Emirates Stadium.Indeed, according to well-placed sources there has been a slight softening of Alvarez's stance in recent days, although not enough yet to get anyone at Arsenal excited.But should he change his mind in the final days of the window, then the Gunners are poised.Since the start of the summer, according to BBC Sport sources, Arsenal have been confident Alvarez's move to Barcelona was a non-starter.But while he still harboured hope of fulfilling that ambition, Arteta's men focused on the captures of Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa, while also trying to bring Real Madrid attacker Vinicius Jr to London.With the Brazilian extending his contract to stay in Spain, Arsenal have now decided to step things up regarding Alvarez.Atleti director Mateu Alemany was in London last week, where he is understood to have met with Arsenal counterparts - and made clear his side would seek a fee of 150m euros (£128m). The Gunners are confident they can finance any deal and quickly finalise the transfer - if he said yes.Arteta is fully aware if Alvarez was to join Arsenal this summer he would only be doing so because his preferred destination was not possible.It is understood the Spaniard is comfortable with that scenario and believes Alvarez would eventually become fully invested and committed to the Arsenal project.The ball is now in Alvarez's court. If he wants to leave Atletico, which sources close to the attacker insist that he does, then the Premier League champions appear to be his only option.Alvarez joined Atletico for £81m from Manchester City in August 2024, having spent just over two years at the Etihad following a £14.1 move from Argentine side River Plate.He won six major trophies at City - including the Treble of Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in 2023 - scoring 36 goals in 106 appearances.At Atletico, he has scored 49 goals in 107 appearances, but has not yet won any silverware.Could Alvarez also concede defeat in his efforts to leave Atleti this summer and attempt to mend what appears to be a broken relationship with the club and its supporters?It is possible, although, according to those close to the player, it is his belief that the Madrid club are being unreasonable. Indeed the player's agent Fernando Hidalgo has been open with his disdain towards how his client has been treated this summer.That said, Alvarez is described as a private individual and said to be deeply uncomfortable about the very public nature of the conflict with his club - although the player himself also outlined his desire to leave publicly during the World Cup."A transfer is the best option," he said.When Real Madrid released a statement on 9 June saying they had an offer of 150m euros (£128m) rejected by their neighbours, there was a sense from the Alvarez camp Atletico had reneged on an agreement to let the striker leave if they received an offer of that amount.Of course, the prospect of selling Alvarez to their fiercest rivals was viewed as a non-starter by Atletico.For South Americans - playing for Real or Barca represents the holy grail.Hansi Flick's side remain interested in Alvarez, but fear Atletico's stance isn't purely posturing and have started to consider alternative options, including Arsenal's Swedish striker Viktor Gyokeres.If they decide to turn their attention elsewhere, Alvarez will have a decision to make.Arsenal or nothing? We'll have the answer soon.
